extracted.intended_audience: courtiers, gentlemen, and readers learning Renaissance courtly conduct and wit
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and standards for producing tasteful pleasantries and practical jokes at court: when and how to provoke laughter, appropriate techniques, limits (rank, persons, frequency), and the distinction between clever jesting and knavery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cheat expectation (surprise)
rubrics_metrics.description: The main thing is to cheat expectation and reply otherwise than the hearer looks for.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applies to both verbal pleasantry and actions: arouse laughter by doing or saying something contrary to expectation. May be 'seasoned' with deceit, dissimulation, ridicule, censure, simile, or other styles. Examples throughout the text (e.g., Altoviti answering with the opposite; practical jokes that first excite alarm then turn out well).

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider time, persons, and rank
rubrics_metrics.description: The Courtier pays heed to time, persons and his own rank in his banter and amusing talk.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not use pleasantry inappropriately for the moment or audience; adapt content and force to the social status of interlocutors. Failure to consider these leads to offence or impropriety; repeated or out-of-season pleasantry begets tedium.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moderation and avoidance of spite
rubrics_metrics.description: Take care not to be so sharp and biting as to be thought spiteful, assailing causelessly or with evident rancour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid attacking recklessly: attacking those too powerful is imprudent, attacking the too weak is cruel, attacking the too wicked is useless, and offending people you would not wish to offend is ignorance. Pleasantry must not be spiteful or vengeful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protect women's honour; show reverence to women
rubrics_metrics.description: The Courtier's practical jokes and pleasantries should pay respect and reverence to women, especially where their honour may be touched.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tarnishing a noble lady's honour is an evil act worthy of severe punishment; because accusations against women cause lasting disgrace, courtiers should avoid jokes that attack female chastity or reputation. Practical jokes must not be allowed to degenerate into offences against women.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not overuse pleasantry
rubrics_metrics.description: Use pleasantries and amusing talk not too often; constant joking in all conversation in season and out begets tedium.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Limit frequency to avoid wearing out the effect. Practical implication: intersperse seriousness and be sparing so humour retains freshness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adapt delivery: patience, gravity, and tempo
rubrics_metrics.description: Some witticisms need an air of patience and are slowly uttered with a certain gravity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Slow, grave delivery can make a witticism keener; examples include the rustic/Cato exchange. Use tempo deliberately to heighten effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Match gestures and facial expression to humour
rubrics_metrics.description: The Courtier must adapt his behaviour, gestures and face to his pleasantry; the graver and more impassive his face, the spicier his sallies will seem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Nonverbal comportment is part of successful wit: a serious countenance can sharpen the comic contrast. Train natural aptitude for humorous expression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Season pleasantry with rhetorical devices (metaphor, simile, hidden meaning)
rubrics_metrics.description: Pleasantry is enhanced by metaphors, similes, or using words with hidden meaning remote from the apparent intention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use metaphors seasonably (examples: Marcantonio and Bottone). Employ double meanings or concealed senses to enrich the jest (example: Prefect saying 'It must be new'). Avoid obvious or crude figures that detract from elegance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider hearers' state of mind and health
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider our hearers' state of mind, for to the afflicted jocosity often brings greater affliction, and there are certain maladies that are aggravated the more medicine is employed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid joking with people who are distressed, ill, or otherwise vulnerable; what amuses one may wound another. Tailor humour sensitively to audience condition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid vulgarity and grossness
rubrics_metrics.description: Pleasantries vary: some have a taint of grossness or move to blush as well as laugh; avoid coarse or scurrilous forms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courtly humour should favor elegance and modest pleasantness over grossness; practical jokes of courtiers should be farther removed from scurrility and knavery common among rogues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cleverness and discretion in practical jokes
rubrics_metrics.description: Practical joking is friendly deceit in things that do not offend or that offend only a little; the cleverer and more discreet these jokes are, the more they please and are applauded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A successful practical joke should be skillful and discreet; reckless joking often gives offence and leads to enmity. Examples: tricks played courteously at court that cause hearty laughter without lasting harm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish two kinds of practical jokes
rubrics_metrics.description: One kind tricks someone cleverly in a fine and amusing manner; the other casts a net and offers a little bait so that the victim hastens to be tricked.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Both forms exist and can be used appropriately; baiting-type jokes risk deeper humiliation if mishandled. Prefer clever, refined tricks for a courtier's esteem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid practical jokes that become knavery or money extortion
rubrics_metrics.description: Care must be taken not to let practical joking degenerate into knavery, as in rogues who use wiles to get money by pretending one thing and then another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain ethical boundary: jokes must not be cover for fraud or theft. Examples of anti-patterns: a physician extorting money by false cure promises; Ponzio tricking peasant out of capons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pleasantry may include self-deprecation
rubrics_metrics.description: We laugh when a man admits everything that is said to him and more too, but pretends to take it in a different sense, or when a man accuses himself of some fault humourously.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strategic self-accusation or mock misunderstanding can produce humour (examples: chaplain pleading he doesn't recite a third of prayers; Biagino saying 'After I have had the priest killed...'). Use sparingly and cleverly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of opposite/contrary replies with artful hesitation
rubrics_metrics.description: A spicy style is to reply the opposite of what the person desires, but slowly and with an air of doubtful and hesitating deliberation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: King Alfonso's ironic denials leading to gifts; the pope's evasive reply. This technique works well for grave and dignified persons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer jokes that end well for the victim
rubrics_metrics.description: Jokes that at first excite alarm and turn out well in the end are especially amusing; the victim often laughs at himself once fear is past.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design pranks so that the victim's dignity is restored and can laugh with others; avoid pranks that produce lasting shame or anger (examples: the inn-blindness prank ends with relief and vows).

rubrics_metrics.name: Select humour types that produce desired secondary effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Pleasantries not only provoke laughter but produce other effects—elegance and modest pleasantness, hidden or open sting, taint of grossness, blushing, or anger.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose the type of jest according to the intended secondary effect: if wanting gentle amusement, aim for elegance and modesty; if teasing a little, a hidden sting may be used—but be aware of consequences and audience.
